chunks: And Abu Jafar (peace be upon him) said:

During the time of the Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him), a man was found slaughtered in a deserted place, and there was a man holding a knife stained with blood. He was taken to be brought before the Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him), and he confessed that he had killed him. Then a man approached them and said, 'Release this one, for I am the one who killed your companion.' He was also taken and brought with his companion before the Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him). When they entered, they recounted the story to him, and he said to the first man, 'What compelled you to confess?'

He said, 'O Commander of the Faithful, I am a butcher, and I had slaughtered a sheep beside the deserted place. Urination hurried me, so I entered the deserted place with a knife in my hand stained with blood. These people took me and said,

Then Ali (peace be upon him) said to the other, 'What do you say?' He said, 'I killed him, O Commander of the Faithful.' The Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) said, 'Go to my son Hasan so that he may judge between you.'

So they went to him and recounted the story to him. He (peace be upon him) said, 'As for this one, if he has killed a man, he has given life to this one (the butcher). And Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says:
ai.seo_question: How did Imam Ali and Imam Hasan resolve a double murder confession case in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This narrative, recorded in *Man La Yahduruhu al-Faqih*, illustrates the principle of *al-dam bi al-dam* (life for life) and the strategic use of circumstantial evidence (*qara'in*) in Shia jurisprudence. Imam al-Baqir (as) highlights how Imam Hasan (as) applied a nuanced legal reasoning where the butcher’s confession, though technically a valid claim to his own life, was accepted as sufficient to spare the actual killer, demonstrating the flexibility of judicial discretion (*ijtihad*) in early Imami legal theory.
